en: Bakai stirred up an uproar.
He was a weather-conjuring hero himself;
He cast a spell upon the weather,
Sending hail upon the foothills.
From the sixty Russian surveyors,
From the hands of the surveyors,
He seized Akkelte back.
Khan Bakai brought it about;
Only with great difficulty was it recovered.
From the Russian khan's city,
Akkelte was taken as booty.
That is the treasure left by Manas,
That is the keen weapon for you to fire.
Upon the yurt's lattice frame,
When your mother met with sorrow,
It was left behind, parted from us.
In the hands of Köbösh Khan.
When you enter, Akkelte
Will bleed from its ear;
It will kick against the lattice,
Booming all by itself,
Cracking all by itself.
Say, “It is my inheritance from my father,”
Ask for it as a gift and bring it back.
If he will not give it when asked,
If he will not heed your words,
Come back without quarreling.
“Mother, he would not give it,”
Come tell this wretched woman.
There is another wonder yet;
Again, orphan, lend your ear,
Understand what I tell you.
Your father Manas was a lion;
The one God, a soul like your father,
Will never create again.
He was a dark, dauntless lion;
His fortune lacked for nothing.
When I tell it through my weeping,
My words to Allah are lamentation.
In the desert of Mediyan,
Upon the pass of Kaiypchy,
Encountered by chance,
For your father Sultan Manas,
Found through the unseen powers,
Were six keen steels that came from heaven.
The mightiest and finest of swords:
Zulpukor, which your father took;
Bakai Khan's Joibolot;
Kylbolot, which Ajybai took;
Almambet's Joikuma;
Tashkeser, which Chubak took;
The sword with a bent tip—
Hero Syrgak's Arkesken.
Those were the six keen blades of steel;
For mortal human beings,
Such treasures could not be found.
When one's stiff, wretched back
Was bent, one drew it;
When one's poor, palm-sized life
Was hard pressed, one drew it.
When upon the earth the dark
Night fell, one drew it;
When one's thoroughly valiant, poor life
Was hard pressed, one drew it.
When the cruel ordeal, the narrow path,
Was faced, one drew it;
When every means was exhausted,
When facing death, one drew it.
When drawn from its sheath with a cry,
It bit into stone when striking it.
Unless well sated with blood,
It would not enter its sheath to be put away.
When swung in wrath,
It never went idle without drinking blood.
When drawn from its sheath with a cry,
It reddened in many shades;
With every swing it grew longer.
Striking stone, it did not recoil;
It did not turn back from iron.
When they plundered my possessions,
When those dogs wrought havoc,
When they thoroughly got the better of me,
With you, orphan, beneath my arm,
When they slashed my breast open,
On a journey of six months,
My dark eyes clouded with grief,
It was left behind, my foal,
In the hands of Abyke.
Speak softly, plead with him,
Beg him, calling him “Uncle,”
Offer him smooth words;
Coax and cajole that villain,
That utterly coarse, wicked man,
Saying, “It is my inheritance from my father,”
Ask for the six keen blades and bring them back.
If he will not give them, my only one,
Come back without quarreling.
“He would not give them at all,”
Come tell me, your wretched mother.
Such is the story of the six blades;
Let me leave that here.
There is another wonder beyond it;
Pay heed, my son, let me begin.
An inheritance left by your father Manas,
Tried and known to every soul:
When he shattered Omsk and took booty,
Broke through its midst and opened a road,
When he struck the Oirat people,
A gray saddlebag came as booty.
Many of your treasures lie within it.
Thus I dedicated them to you,
The allure of this wretched world's riches.
At the bottom of that saddlebag
Is your mother Chyiyrdy's burial shroud.
Say, “It is an heirloom from my father,”
Ask for it as a gift and bring it back.
Do not begrudge the burden, my foal;
Load it upon Aktulpar and bring it back.
There are further words I have to tell;
Hear my words again!
Akolpok, left by your father,
Must have fallen into their hands.
Some coarse dog raised a commoner
Must have put it on carelessly.
Its warp was threaded through with silk;
If worn to a joust, my foal,
It blunted the point of a spear.
No arrow could reach through it;
No musket ball could pierce it.
Its collar was gold, its sleeves copper,
Double mail, its rings like larks' eyes,
A coat with gold-braided trim and a broad collar,
Unwavering when worn in strife—
Your father's Akolpok.
When he went to face the enemy,
When your father campaigned against Beijing,
The bloody scourge Shypshaidar,
The mighty giant of the Chinese,
Tiken the giant, son of Muzkindik,
Who spared no one he fought,
An exceedingly gluttonous great champion,
Whom the flesh of a whole pig
Could not sate at a single meal,
Who laid low whoever appeared,
With a cast-iron mace of twelve batmans
Bound snugly to his waist,
Muzkindik and Orokkyr,
Six thousand Chinese, countless kaldais,
And Kongurbai, the finest of them all—
When the giants pressed hard upon him,
Forty thousand champions, many Chinese,
Your father, favored by Khidr,
They closed in around.
They loosed arrows like rain;
They fired shot like hail.
Standing tall, they shouted their battle-cries;
The forty tribes of the Chinese, the separate peoples,
Shouted each apart.
Each of those peoples
Called its own battle-cry.
Like reeds, they formed a flood,
With the mighty Kongurbai,
An engulfing mass of Chinese people,
Swaying in ranks along the edge,
Heaving as they stood side by side.
The sky was clear, the earth overcast;
Not a speck of ground could be seen.
Mist covered the face of the earth;
Not a single person could be seen.
Kongurbai, a cultivator of wisdom,
Isolated your father.
There was no Almambet, Chubak, or Syrgak,
Amid the seething Chinese,
When he was trapped in their siege,
With coral hat-buttons and jeweled stones,
The khan of the lungtungs among them,
Your dauntless father Manas
They encircled.
Among unbelievers swarming like ants,
Your wretched father, the dauntless hero,
Was caught in their midst.
All the spear-bearers,
Making blows thud upon your father,
Thrust at him with their spears.
Your father Manas, looming huge,
Was caught in the center.
For six days your father was besieged;
The Chinese surrounded him.
The red sword Zulpukor,
And Akolpok, fitted snugly upon him—
Against bloody spears and guns,
Akolpok held firm.
The points of spears bent;
Musket shot failed to pierce, cannon shot fell away;
Akolpok held firm.
No cunning device could prevail;
The edge of Arkesken could not reach your father.
In the clash with Khakanchyn,
With the massed Chinese and Manchus,
In the blood-spilling battle,
Akolpok held firm.
When fired, musket balls could not pierce it;
When thrust ruthlessly, spears could not pierce it.
Unable to withstand your father's fury,
The Chinese fled in confusion.
“His coat is made of steel!”
Kongurbai, khan of the monks,
Marveled at that coat of your father's.
I, your luckless mother,
Worked its lining in silk,
Taking no rest by day,
Taking no sleep at night,
Biting at it tirelessly for seven years.
From staring at it,
My dear eyes grew weary;
From biting at it,
My dear teeth wore away.
When upon the khoja of Kokand
He inflicted humiliation,
To the petition officer in Bukhara,
When he laid down his commands,
When upon the khoja of Andijan
He wrought dreadful deeds,
Upon Alty-Shaar and Margilan
He inflicted humiliation.
Upon the lands that would not obey,
Your mighty father Manas fixed his gaze
And used his force.
Throughout the face of the earth, tumult
He stirred in those days;
From every land he reached, tribute
He took in those days.
Between Orenburg and Margilan,
I, your unfortunate mother,
Had the intervening lands searched.
All the fine cloth from there to here
I had brought by force.
When did your mother ever sleep?
Not one day did she go outside.
To bring the fine cloth,
Your mother dispatched forty falcons of men.
I had white fine cloth brought;
Of filings from hard iron,
The finest, like sand, I had sifted.
Layering them eightyfold again and again,
I had them put into Akolpok.
Without shrinking, I sewed and toiled;
Without tiring of the sewing, working long,
Only in eight years did I finish it.
Then, when they plundered my possessions,
Accursed be widowhood!
When that coarse dog, roaring,
Broke into the palace,
That precious thing went as booty.
Most precious of all, my son,
When you enter, upon the golden throne,
